name: Stacking
summary: Stacking is lining both partners up on the same side before the ball is struck, then moving to the positions you actually want once it is. It exists so a pair can keep the same player on the same side of the court all game — most often to keep two forehands in the middle, or a left-hander's forehand there.
whenToUse: One of you is left-handed, so both forehands can cover the middle.
One partner is clearly stronger and you want them on the side more balls come to.
One of you has a backhand you would rather hide from the middle.
You are comfortable enough with the score and the positions not to get confused.
howTo: Decide before the game which side each of you wants to finish on, and stay with it.
When serving, the server stands where the score requires; the partner stands on the side they want to end up on.
The server crosses to their preferred side immediately after contact.
When returning, the non-returner stands off the court on the side they want, and the returner crosses after hitting.
Call it out. A quiet stack is how a team ends up with both players in one service court.
If it goes wrong mid-game, stop stacking rather than trying to fix it point by point.
commonMistakes: Stacking without agreeing the target positions first, so both of you cross to the same place.
Forgetting the server still has to stand in the correct service court — stacking does not change the serving rules.
Getting the score wrong and stacking off the wrong side, which is a fault waiting to happen.
Stacking every point when only the return side actually needed it.
Using it to hide a weakness so completely that the weakness never improves.

drills.name: Walk it through, no ball
drills.description: Set the score out loud and walk through the positions for serving and returning, both even and odd. No ball at all. Ten minutes of this saves a whole game of confusion.

drills.name: Stack the return only
drills.description: Play games where you stack on return but not on serve. It is the half that matters most and the half that is hardest to get wrong.
